actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: This species is distributed in the western Atlantic from Cape Canaveral, Florida south along the U.S. coast, Bermuda, the Bahamas, in the Gulf of Mexico from the Florida Keys to the Florida panhandle, the Flower Garden Banks, offshore of Corpus Christi, Texas and from Tuxpan, Mexico along the northern Yucatan Peninsula to northwestern Cuba, throughout the Caribbean Sea, and along the South American coast to Bahia, Brazil including the Fernando de Noronha Islands (R. Robertson pers. comm. 2014). Records from the eastern Atlantic require verification. Its depth range is zero to 50 m.
documentation.population: This species is one of the more common and fairly abundant species of moray in the western Atlantic (D. Smith pers. comm. 2011).
documentation.habitats: This species is found in tidepools, rocks, mangroves and coral reefs and can enter brackish-water tidal creeks and mangrove areas, as well as brackish-water caves. It is primarily nocturnal and hides during the day (Randall 1965). It mainly feeds at night on fish and crustaceans. It is aggressive and its bite can be dangerous to humans. While the flesh of this species is safe, its liver contains high levels of ciguatoxins (Pottier and Vernoux 2003).
documentation.threats: There are no major threats known to this species.
documentation.measures: There are no species-specific conservation measures.
documentation.use_trade: It is rarely caught and marketed due to its toxicity (Vernous and Talha 1989).  Some  individuals are removed and used for display in public aquaria.
documentation.rationale: This species is widely distributed, common and fairly abundant where it occurs in a variety of shallow coastal habitats. There are no known major threats, therefore, it is listed as Least Concern.
